extracted.intended_audience: credit card issuers, industry trade associations, consumer advocates, and legal/regulatory practitioners
extracted.subtask_short: CFPB late fee safe harbor rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and section-by-section discussion of the CFPB's final rule revising Regulation Z safe harbor amounts for penalty fees (especially late fees) for Larger Card Issuers, including the determination to set an $8 late-fee safe harbor and related methodological and policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterrence effect and alternative deterrents
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether lower late fees will meaningfully change consumer payment behavior, taking into account other deterrents and tools issuers can (and increasingly do) use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB expects that increased digital enrollment (online portals, mobile apps, e-statements) and other issuer actions (timely reminders, well-chosen due dates, encouraging automatic payments) reduce the likelihood of missed payments and therefore affect the deterrent role of late fees. Consider evidence of enrollment and use: e.g., 76% enrolled in online portal, 76% in mobile app, 67% receiving only e-statements (2022). Also consider that issuers could offset lower late-fee revenue by increasing interest rates, which may change consumers' incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor must cover pre-charge-off collection costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Set safe harbor late-fee amounts so they cover pre-charge-off collection costs for the average issuer (the statutory limit under the CARD Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB determines the $8 safe harbor will cover pre-charge-off collection costs for the average Larger Card Issuer. When evaluating late-fee amounts, limit consideration of issuer revenue to whether the fee covers pre-charge-off collection costs; do not treat excess late-fee revenue as a subsidy for other products or services. Issuers whose pre-charge-off costs are not fully covered may use the cost analysis provisions in §1026.52(b)(1)(i) to set a higher fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness and proportionality to the actual violation (CARD Act requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Late fees must be reasonable and proportional to the cost of the omission or violation (not to the potential risk posed by a consumer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB concludes permitting risk-based pricing for late fees (setting fees by estimated consumer group risk) is generally inconsistent with the CARD Act because the statute ties late fees to the cost of the omission. The safe harbor is a presumptively reasonable/proportional amount; risk-based pricing could produce fees higher than the cost of the violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use inapt external proxies for fee-setting (e.g., utility, returned-check, student loan fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid relying on unrelated penalty-fee benchmarks under State or sectoral law as proxies for credit-card late-fee deterrence or cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB declines to rely on returned-check penalties, utility late fees, or student loan late fees because those penalties often do not trigger comparable financial consequences (missed grace periods, a month's interest on balances, or new purchase interest) and thus are inapt proxies for deterrence analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of consumer conduct and account-level data (Y-14) in assessing appropriate fee amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze issuer-provided account-level data (e.g., Y-14) to measure how consumers actually behave after incurring a late fee and how quickly accounts return to current status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB used Y-14 data (Oct 2021–Sept 2022) finding: 13.6% of accounts incurred a late fee and then no additional payments were made; ~33% of accounts paid within 5 days, ~50% within 15 days, and ~60% within 30 days. Also consider credit reporting conventions (Metro 2 treats payments within 30 days as not late) when evaluating how serious a late payment is deemed for risk purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish single vs. repeat late payments (six-billing-cycle framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether repeat late payments within the next six billing cycles indicate materially greater credit risk and therefore justify different treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board previously noted repeat late payments over six months present greater credit risk and can be distinguished from single occurrences. CFPB's analysis of Y-14 data suggests it is not clear that multiple violations during a relatively short period are associated with increased credit risk, and the CFPB declines to make the safe-harbor amount reflect a broader conception of increased credit risk than the industry credit-reporting standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative issuer tools for managing credit risk beyond late fees
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing the need for higher late fees, account for other tools issuers may use to manage risk, such as changing APRs, penalty rates, credit-line reductions, and credit bureau reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB notes issuers can: (1) reprice new transactions via penalty rates under §1026.55(b)(3); (2) after 60 days, reprice outstanding balances under §1026.55(b)(4); (3) reduce credit lines; and (4) report late payments to credit bureaus (which generally occurs at 30+ days). These tools can substitute for higher late fees in managing chronic delinquencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-based pricing for late fees is inappropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting late-fee amounts by estimated risk groups is generally inconsistent with the statutory requirement that late fees be based on the actual violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because bona fide late fees are excluded from the finance charge under TILA/Regulation Z, treating them as a price component for risk management is difficult to justify. Risk-based late fees could exceed the cost of the omission and are thus inconsistent with the CARD Act's requirement of reasonableness/proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain special rule for charge cards (3% of delinquent balance after two consecutive cycles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charge card issuers may impose a fee not exceeding 3% of the delinquent balance when payment is missed for two or more consecutive billing cycles, given charge-card accounts typically do not bear periodic interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB preserves this special rule (§1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(C)) because charge cards cannot respond to delinquency by increasing an APR. CFPB did not lower this particular safe-harbor amount and clarifies that the rule applies only where no periodic rate is used to compute a finance charge (per §1026.2(a)(15)(iii)). Examples in commentary are updated to use the $8 late-fee amount for consistency elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of cost-analysis route to set higher fees (§1026.52(b)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuers can opt to calculate a cost-basis late fee using the cost analysis provision instead of relying on the safe harbor amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB expects some Larger Card Issuers will use §1026.52(b)(1)(i) to set fees; CFPB disagrees this is an undue operational burden for sophisticated issuers, which should be able to track pre-charge-off collection costs and perform the necessary calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor is discretionary; elimination considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that establishing a safe harbor is an exercise of discretionary rulemaking authority and that eliminating the safe harbor is legally permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB considered comments proposing elimination of the safe harbor (arguing for simplicity) and industry opposition noting complexity and consumer uncertainty; CFPB decided to repeal the current safe harbor amounts for Larger Card Issuers and adopt a new $8 safe harbor rather than eliminate the concept entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid complex/staggered fee structures (opposed by commenters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not adopt staggered-per-day small fees accumulating to a cap or similarly complex fee mechanisms due to implementation, cost, and consumer-confusion concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters uniformly opposed staggered fee proposals as adding complexity, expense, and confusion; CFPB declined to adopt such approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions on using the safe harbor (autopay or additional notices) — considered but not adopted
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether to require issuers to offer autopay or provide additional notices as a precondition to relying on the safe harbor; weighed consumer-protection benefits against legal authority and burden concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some consumer groups supported conditioning the safe harbor on offering autopay and mailing notices before charging late fees to online-statement-only customers. Industry opposed these prerequisites citing legal limits (TILA), increased compliance costs, TCPA and state-law complications, and lack of data demonstrating effectiveness. CFPB declines to impose such conditions but may revisit in the future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not extend $8 safe harbor to all penalty fees absent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from lowering safe harbor amounts for other penalty fees (over-the-limit, returned-payment, declined access check) until sufficient data justify doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry commenters opposed extending $8 to all penalty fees and provided no data; consumer groups supported broader reductions. CFPB declines to extend $8 because late fees are the most prevalent and available evidence primarily relates to late fees charged by Larger Card Issuers. CFPB will monitor the market for changes in prevalence of other penalty fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual CPI-W adjustment procedure for threshold amounts (§1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the non-late-fee penalty safe harbor threshold amounts annually using the CPI-W (Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers) in effect on the preceding June 1, increasing or decreasing the amounts by $1 if the cumulative change equals a whole dollar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB applies the established Regulation Z method for annual adjustments: if cumulative CPI-W-derived adjusted value rises/decreases by a whole dollar, amounts are increased/decreased by $1. CFPB updated §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(A) and (B) to $32 and $43 respectively (reflecting CPI-W changes from Apr 2021→Apr 2022 and Apr 2022→Apr 2023) and amended commentary to preserve historical thresholds and conform citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different treatment for Smaller Card Issuers
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller Card Issuers (affiliates together fewer than one million open credit card accounts in the preceding calendar year) are not covered by the $8 safe harbor adopted for Larger Card Issuers and may use the safe harbors provided in §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(A) and (B) as revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB emphasizes that the CARD Act permits recovery of only pre-charge-off costs; in setting the $8 safe harbor it considered revenue effects only for covering pre-charge-off collection costs. Smaller issuers retain alternative safe harbor amounts; CFPB also notes potential burdens (e.g., autopay outsourcing) raised by smaller institutions when considering new prerequisites.
